sections.h: The book of Joel in outline
sections.b: Joel is three chapters in English (four in Hebrew). Chapter 1 describes a plague of locusts, a drought and the stopping of the Temple offerings, and calls the nation to mourn. Chapter 2 sounds the alarm of the day of the LORD, calls everyone to turn back, and reports the LORD's answer: the land restored, the Spirit poured out on all flesh, and rescue for those who call on his name. Chapter 3 shows the nations judged in the Valley of Jehoshaphat and Zion blessed. The book names no king and gives no date. It is read at the border of prophecy and apocalyptic, and it is the source of the passage Peter quotes at Pentecost.

sections.h: Joel in the Twelve, and in worship
sections.b: In the Hebrew order Joel stands between Hosea and Amos; in the Greek order it stands after Micah. Joel 3:16 and 3:18 are word for word, or nearly, Amos 1:2 and 9:13, and Joel 2:13 is shared with Jonah 4:2. Joel 2:12-18 is the Ash Wednesday reading of the Catholic church, Joel 2:1-2, 12-17 is the Ash Wednesday reading of the common lectionary, and Joel 2:28-32 is the heart of Peter's sermon at Pentecost. The Mishnah quotes Joel 2:13 in its order for public fasts for rain.

common: The prophet Joel is a post-exilic voice (most critical scholars) who reads the prophets before him and uses a locust plague as the sign of the day of the LORD.
uncommon: Joel is a very early prophet from the ninth century, in the time of the boy-king Joash and the priest Jehoiada (Stuart), which would make it the oldest of the writing prophets.

sections.h: Joel's locusts: four names and an army
sections.b: No book of the Bible has more to say about locusts than Joel. Chapter 1 names four kinds (the cutting, swarming, hopping and stripping locust) and describes a plague that stripped vine, fig, grain and pasture. Chapter 2 pictures what is probably the same insects as a mighty army that climbs walls and enters houses like a thief, led by the LORD himself (2:11) and called his 'great army' in 2:25. Readers have taken the book as a real plague, a human army told in locust language, or a picture of the end of days.

Locusts are one of the curses of the covenant (Deuteronomy 28:38, 42), one of the troubles Solomon prays about (1 Kings 8:37) and one of the plagues of Egypt (Exodus 10:1-20; Psalm 78:46; Psalm 105:34-35). Proverbs 30:27 admires their order ("the locusts have no king, but out they go in rows, every one of them"), and Nahum 3:15-17 compares Nineveh's officials to locusts that fly away. Revelation 9:1-11 builds its scorpion locusts out of Joel 1-2: the shape of horses, teeth like lions, a noise like chariots.

common: The locusts of Joel 1 are real insects, and 2:1-11 either continues the plague or describes it by comparison with an army.
uncommon: The four locusts are four empires, and the plague is a veiled history (Jerome reports this as a Jewish reading).

sections.h: Joel's five days of the LORD
sections.b: The phrase occurs five times in Joel: 'the day of the LORD is close' (1:15), 'the day of the LORD is coming' (2:1), 'the day of the LORD is great and very awesome' (2:11), 'the great and awesome day of the LORD' (2:31) and 'the day of the LORD is near in the valley of decision' (3:14). The meaning grows. At first it is the plague and the invading army (1:15; 2:1-11), a day of darkness and cloud. Then it is the day on which the LORD offers rescue to those who turn (2:12-14, 32). Then it is the day of cosmic signs and the Spirit (2:28-31), and lastly the day on which the nations are judged (3:12-16). The day is a day of the LORD's own presence, and its effect depends on whether people turn to him.

sections.h: Where the day of the LORD comes from
sections.b: Three explanations are common. Gerhard von Rad derived the day from the old holy wars of Israel, the day when the LORD fought for his people. Sigmund Mowinckel connected it to an autumn festival of the LORD's kingship. Meir Weiss, reading Amos 5:18-20, argued that it comes from the tradition of the LORD appearing in storm and fire. Amos reverses the hope: for those who longed for the day it would be darkness, not light. Joel keeps the darkness and cloud (2:2) but adds the offer of turning back and the promise of rescue on Zion (2:32).

common: In Joel the day of the LORD is at once a present disaster, a call to repent and a future judgment of the nations; the nearness of the day is the book's argument for turning back.
uncommon: Joel's day of the LORD is a single, repeated event of the same kind (plague, army, nations) rather than an end of the world.

claude.title: Claude's theory: the day grows with each use
claude.body: My own observation: the five uses are not five repetitions but a staircase. Each time the phrase is used it has a larger scene and a larger audience: a farmland (1:15), a city (2:1), a nation at prayer (2:11), the sky (2:31), the world's nations (3:14). Readers who ask whether Joel's 'day' is past or future may be asking one question too many; the book may be showing a day that is always arriving, each time bigger. Commentators have noticed the five uses (Crenshaw lists them) but I know no one who sets them out as a staircase.

sections.b: Joel calls for a fast three times (1:14; 2:12; 2:15). In 1:14 the priests and elders are to 'consecrate a fast' and call a sacred assembly at the house of the LORD; in 2:12 the LORD himself asks for a return 'with fasting, with weeping and with mourning', and then adds that the heart, not the clothes, must be torn (2:13); in 2:15-16 the whole community is gathered, from the elders to the nursing babies and the bridegroom. It is the fullest picture in the prophets of a public fast, and it shaped the Mishnah's rules for fasts in time of drought (Taanit 1-3) and the Christian Lent, whose first day opens with Joel 2:12-18.

Joel 2:12-14 is one of the prophets' clearest calls to repentance. It begins with the LORD's own word, 'Even now', and it names the form: turning back with the whole heart, with fasting, weeping and mourning. It then rejects display (tear your hearts, not your clothes) and gives the reason: the LORD is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, great in loyal love, and he changes his mind about the harm. The ending does not promise: 'Who knows? He may turn back and change his mind.' Repentance is a plea made to a God who owes nothing and may give much.

Joel and Jonah share a line, 'he changes his mind about the harm', which each adds to the creed of Exodus 34:6-7. In Joel the line gives the reason for hope that the plague and its army can be turned back; in Jonah it is the reason Jonah ran. In both the point is the same: God's threats are open to change when people turn, and this is part of his character, not a weakness. Joel then asks 'Who knows?', in the voice of David on his sick child (2 Samuel 12:22), so that the LORD's freedom to relent is not turned into a promise that can be claimed.

sections.b: Joel 2:13 quotes the creed in which the LORD is 'great in loyal love'. The Plain English Translation's 'loyal love' is the Hebrew hesed, a love bound by a promise. In Joel it sits beside 'gracious and compassionate' and 'slow to anger', and it is the reason the prophet gives for hope. Unlike Exodus 34:6, Joel does not add 'faithfulness' and leaves out the second half about the guilty; the creed is cut to the part the moment needs.

sections.h: Joel 2:28-29: the Spirit on all flesh
sections.b: In the Hebrew Bible the Spirit of the LORD came on particular people for particular tasks: judges, kings, craftsmen and prophets. Moses wished that all the LORD's people were prophets (Numbers 11:29). Joel promises it: 'I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh', on sons and daughters, old and young, even slaves, and they will prophesy, dream and see visions. Ezekiel 39:29 and Isaiah 44:3 use the same verb, 'pour out', for the Spirit. Peter quotes Joel at Pentecost, as the sign that the last days have begun (Acts 2:16-21).
sections.refs: Joel 2:28-29; Numbers 11:29; Isaiah 44:3; Ezekiel 39:29; Acts 2:16-21; Acts 2:39

common: Joel promises the Spirit to all the people, without distinction of age, sex or rank, in the age to come.
uncommon: 'All flesh' means only the people of Israel (the earlier part of the verse names sons, daughters, old men, young men and slaves), and the church's use of it for all nations is an extension.

sections.b: Joel 2:28 says 'after this' in the Hebrew, and the Greek Bible says 'after these things'. When Peter quotes the passage in Acts 2:17 he says 'in the last days', placing the outpouring at the start of the last days. The prophets' 'last days' or 'latter days' (Isaiah 2:2; Hosea 3:5; Ezekiel 38:16) are the time when God acts decisively; Joel's stages (restoration of the land, the Spirit, the judgment of the nations) run through them.

Joel opens with the formula 'the word of the LORD came' (1:1), and he is both a prophet and a liturgist, writing prayers for the priests to say (2:17). The book also looks forward to the end of the prophet as a special class: 'your sons and your daughters will prophesy' (2:28). Scholars have asked whether Joel was a Temple prophet, a scribe interpreting earlier prophecy (Bergler), or a literary figure.

Joel 2:32 says that on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem 'there will be survivors', and that among those who are left are the ones the LORD calls. The words peletah, 'survivors', and sarid, 'one who is left', are two of the remnant words of the prophets. Obadiah 17 repeats the first. The remnant here is the safe place inside the judgment, not a leftover after it.

Joel 1 is built as a call to lament, addressed in turn to elders, drunkards, farmers, vinedressers and priests, with a prayer in the voice of one person at the end (1:19-20). It uses the features of the community lament: description of ruin, a call to wail, the cry of the day of the LORD, and an appeal to God. It has no confession of sin; the chapter asks for mourning and the next chapter for turning back.

sections.h: Wine cut off and wine poured out
sections.b: Wine opens and closes Joel. In 1:5 the drunkards are told to weep because sweet wine is cut off from their mouths; in 1:9 the drink offering is cut off from the house of the LORD; in 2:24 the vats overflow again with new wine; in 3:18 the mountains drip sweet wine. The same Hebrew word, 'asis, is used in 1:5 and 3:18. Joel does not condemn wine; he treats its loss as a loss of joy and of worship.

sections.h: Harvest lost, harvest restored, harvest of the nations
sections.b: Joel uses harvest three ways. In chapter 1 the harvest of the field is lost (1:11, 17). In chapter 2 the threshing floors are full of grain again (2:24) and the lost years are given back (2:25). In chapter 3 the harvest is the nations ripe for judgment: 'Send in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe' (3:13). Revelation 14:14-20 combines the sickle and the winepress of the same verse.

sections.h: Zion in Joel: the horn, the refuge and the home
sections.b: Joel begins the alarm 'in Zion' (2:1), says the survivors will be on Mount Zion (2:32), has the LORD roar from Zion (3:16), and ends with 'the LORD lives in Zion' (3:21). The same city that is under threat is the place of refuge. The word 'holy' is used of the mountain (2:1; 3:17) and of Jerusalem (3:17), which will be a holy place that outsiders will not pass through.
sections.refs: Joel 2:1; Joel 2:32; Joel 3:16-17; Joel 3:21; Amos 1:2; Obadiah 17

sections.b: Joel names Edom and Egypt as the lands to be made waste 'because of the violence against Judah's people'. Edom's part in the sack of Jerusalem is set out in Obadiah 10-14, Psalm 137:7 and Lamentations 4:21-22; Egypt's raids in 1 Kings 14:25 and 2 Kings 23:29. If Joel is early, Edom's revolt under Jehoram (2 Kings 8:20-22) fits; if late, the events of 586 BC.

In Joel Egypt is the first of two nations named for desolation, 'because of the violence against Judah's people'. It stands for the great power to the south that raided Judah (Shishak, 1 Kings 14:25-26) and killed Josiah (2 Kings 23:29). It also recalls the first plague of locusts that came on Egypt (Exodus 10), now with Egypt itself as the waste.

Joel charges Tyre, Sidon and the districts of Philistia with taking the LORD's silver and gold into their temples and selling the people of Judah and Jerusalem to the Greeks, and promises that their children will be sold, by Judah, to Sheba. The slave trade of Tyre is also in Amos 1:9-10 and Ezekiel 27:13. The passage has been used in the dating debate, since it is either the Philistine and Arab raid of 2 Chronicles 21:16-17 or a later event.

Joel calls out 'all the districts of Philistia' with Tyre and Sidon, and the Greek reads 'Galilee of the foreigners'. The five Philistine cities were Judah's neighbors on the coast and, in the days of Jehoram, joined the Arabs in a raid on Jerusalem that carried off the king's family and goods (2 Chronicles 21:16-17).

Joel uses Eden twice. In 2:3 the land before the army is 'like the garden of Eden' and behind it a desolate wilderness; in 3:18 a spring flows from the house of the LORD to water the dry valley, a picture that Ezekiel 47 and Revelation 22 draw on. The garden is first a picture of what will be lost and then of what will return.

sections.h: Joel's locusts and the plagues of Egypt
sections.b: Joel draws on the eighth plague of Egypt (Exodus 10:1-20): the words 'locust' ('arbeh) and 'never before, never again' (Joel 2:2; Exodus 10:14), the call to tell the children (Joel 1:3; Exodus 10:2) and the phrase 'you will know that I am the LORD' (Joel 2:27; Exodus 10:2). In Joel the plague is again the LORD's act, but the nation is called to turn back, not to be hardened.

Joel assumes a working Temple. The daily offerings stop for lack of grain and wine (1:9, 13), the priests serve at the altar (1:13), the priests stand 'between the porch and the altar' to pray (2:17), a spring will come from the house of the LORD (3:18), and the LORD lives in Zion (3:17, 21). The Temple is where the nation turns to the LORD and where his blessing is meant to come from.

Joel blows the shofar twice: as an alarm (2:1) and to call the fast and assembly (2:15). The same horn serves both warning and gathering, as in Numbers 10 and Jeremiah 4:5. Joel 2:1 shows its use as the signal of the day of the LORD, a use the New Testament picks up in the trumpet of 1 Thessalonians 4:16 and Revelation 8-11.

sections.h: Calling on the name of the LORD
sections.b: Joel 2:32 says that everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be rescued. The Hebrew name is YHWH. In Acts 2:21 Peter ends his quotation of Joel with this verse, and in Romans 10:9-13 Paul quotes it with 'Lord' meaning Jesus, since the Greek translation put 'Lord' (kyrios) for the divine name. Jewish readers keep the original sense: to call on God by his name in Jerusalem is to be delivered.

Joel promises that 'your old men will have dreams, and your young men will see visions'. In the law, dreams and visions are two of the ways the LORD speaks to a prophet (Numbers 12:6). Joel gives them to all ages, not only prophets. Acts 2:17 quotes the verse with the order of old and young reversed.

Joel mentions slaves twice. In 2:29 the male and female slaves are among those on whom the LORD pours out his Spirit, which puts them on the same footing as sons, daughters, old men and young men. In 3:3 and 3:6-8 the nations are charged with selling the people of Judah, and are told that their own children will be sold in return. The book thus sees slavery from the side of the slave in both places.

Joel accuses Tyre, Sidon and Philistia of selling the people of Judah and Jerusalem 'to the Greeks', literally 'the sons of the Ionians'. It is a rare mention of Greeks in the prophets. Greek traders were on the Syrian coast from about the eighth century BC. The date of Joel hangs partly on this verse, because it is easy to place Greek slave buyers in the Persian period and harder, though not impossible, in the ninth century.

Joel 3:9 tells the nations 'Consecrate war!', using the verb for setting something apart as holy, the same verb as 'consecrate a fast' in 1:14. In ancient Israel a war began with sacrifice and prayer (1 Samuel 7:9; 13:9-12). Jeremiah 6:4 and Micah 3:5 use the phrase for a war against Jerusalem. Joel turns it into a summons to a battle in which the LORD is judge.

sections.h: The judgment of the nations in Joel 3
sections.b: Joel's judgment of the nations is not a series of oracles against named peoples, as in Isaiah 13-23 or Amos 1-2, but a single scene: all the nations gathered, tried and judged in the Valley of Jehoshaphat. Only Tyre, Sidon, Philistia, Egypt and Edom are named. The charges are the same as in the oracles: the harm done to the LORD's people, with a punishment that matches the crime.

sections.h: Turning the fortunes of Judah and Jerusalem
sections.b: Joel 3:1 uses the idiom shuv shevut, 'turn the fortunes around', for the reversal that begins the judgment of the nations. The same idiom is used of the return from Babylon (Jeremiah 29:14; 30:3; 33:7) and of Job's restoration (Job 42:10). Scholars who date Joel after the exile read 3:1-2 as looking back on the scattering of Judah; those who date it earlier read it as the end of a raid.

Joel 3:2 and 3:12 name 'the Valley of Jehoshaphat' as the place where the LORD brings all the nations to judgment. The name means 'the LORD judges.' No valley of that name appears elsewhere in the Bible. It has been taken as a symbolic name, as the valley of Beracah where King Jehoshaphat won a battle (2 Chronicles 20:26), as the Kidron Valley east of Jerusalem, and as the scene of the final judgment. In 3:14 the same valley is called 'the valley of decision'.

sections.h: Joel's signs in sun, moon and stars
sections.b: Joel pictures the sun, moon and stars three times (2:10, 2:30-31, 3:15). At the army's coming the sun and moon grow dark and the stars draw back their light; before the day of the LORD the sun changes into darkness and the moon into blood; at the judgment of the nations the sun and moon grow dark again. Acts 2:19-20 quotes the second of these, and Revelation 6:12 and Matthew 24:29 take up the picture.
sections.refs: Joel 2:10; Joel 2:30-31; Joel 3:15; Acts 2:19-20; Matthew 24:29; Revelation 6:12

sections.h: Joel 3:10 and the reversal of the peace saying
sections.b: Isaiah 2:4 and Micah 4:3 say that in the last days the nations will pound their swords into plowshares. Joel 3:10 says the opposite: 'Pound your plowshares into swords and your pruning knives into spears.' The summons is to war before the judgment. Which text came first is disputed. The reversal makes Joel a darker partner to the peace sayings and shows that the same images were open to use in more than one way.

sections.h: Joel and the beginnings of apocalyptic
sections.b: Joel is often placed between classical prophecy and apocalyptic writing. The day of the LORD is a cosmic event (2:10, 30-31; 3:15), the nations are gathered for a final judgment (3:2, 12), and the enemy in 2:20 is a mysterious 'northern one'. But Joel has no heavenly journey, no angel interpreter and no sealed book, and its call to repent and fast keeps it close to the older prophets.

Joel gives the priests a leading role. They are told to put on sackcloth and spend the night in it (1:13), to lead the fast (1:14), and to weep between the porch and the altar and say the prayer of 2:17. They are called 'those who serve the LORD' (1:9, 13; 2:17). The book never criticizes them.

Joel is second in the Hebrew order (Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah) and fourth in the Greek (Hosea, Amos, Micah, Joel, Obadiah, Jonah). Joel 3:16 repeats Amos 1:2 and Joel 3:18 comes close to Amos 9:13. Joel 2:13 shares its creed with Jonah 4:2, and the day of the LORD and the survivors on Mount Zion tie Joel to Obadiah 15-17. James Nogalski argued that Joel was written or placed to join Hosea to Amos, with catchwords between Hosea 14 (grain, wine, vine) and Joel 1. Others (Ben Zvi, Barton) doubt that the Twelve were composed as one book.
